Tea vs Coffee by Country, Which One Actually Wins

August 18, 2026 Alex

Key Findings

  • Sri Lanka’s tea supply outweighs its coffee supply by about 225 times per person, the widest gap of any country in 2023
  • More than half of the 170 countries with usable data lean coffee by a factor of 5 or more
  • Turkey and China remain firmly tea dominant even after building two of the world’s fastest growing coffee markets
  • Chile, Senegal, and Ivory Coast flipped from leaning toward tea in 2010 to leaning toward coffee in 2023
  • Argentina and Paraguay’s high tea to coffee ratios reflect yerba mate, not Camellia sinensis tea

Tea and coffee are two of the most popular beverages on the planet. The balance between them varies enormously by country, and it has shifted substantially since 2010.

To visualize these changes, I created the maps below using FAO data.

Sri Lanka stands at one extreme. The average resident’s tea supply outweighs their coffee supply by roughly 225 times, the widest gap of any country in 2023.

Coffee vs Tea: 2010 vs 2023

Coffee turns out to be the more common preference by weight. Out of 170 countries with usable data for both drinks in 2023, more than half lean coffee by a factor of 5 or more. Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, and Romania rank near the extreme coffee end of the scale, all supplying more than a hundred times as much coffee as tea per resident. Tea still wins decisively in a smaller group of countries, led by Sri Lanka and Tanzania, both far ahead of the rest of the tea dominant group.

Turkey and China stand out for a different reason. Both built some of the fastest growing coffee markets anywhere over the past decade, yet both remain firmly tea dominant by weight. Coffee has closed real ground in China specifically since 2010, but tea still keeps a wide lead in both countries.

Chile, Senegal, and Ivory Coast all leaned toward tea in 2010 and toward coffee by 2023, a small but genuine shift toward coffee culture in parts of Latin America and Africa. Argentina and Paraguay remain at the tea dominant end of the table throughout, though that reflects yerba mate rather than traditional tea leaves.
